quests.instruction: You phone a company and ask, “Hello, can I speak to Anna?” Which words are weak in the middle of the question?
quests.word: Hello, can I speak to Anna
quests.textToSpeak: Hello, can I speak to Anna
options: “speak” and “Anna” are weak, while “can” and “to” carry the stress
“can” and “to” are weak (/kən/, /tə/), while “speak” and “Anna” carry the stress
All words are equally strong, because phone calls need extra clarity from the speaker
Only “I” is weak; every other word is strong
quests.correctAnswer: “can” and “to” are weak (/kən/, /tə/), while “speak” and “Anna” carry the stress
quests.hint: Tap the beats as a receptionist would hear the question. Which words get the taps?
quests.explanation: Even on the phone, the stress pattern is unchanged: the meaning words “speak” and “Anna” are strong, and “can” and “to” are weak. Knowing where the weight falls helps you catch the name, even when the small words are reduced. Speaking slowly does not remove the weak forms; it only makes them a little longer.
quests.phoneticRule: Even in careful phone speech, function words such as “can” and “to” keep their weak forms, while names and key verbs carry the stress.
quests.spokenForm: Hello, kuhn I speak tuh Anna

quests.instruction: Which pronunciation of “to” fits “I’m calling to confirm the time”?
quests.word: I’m calling to confirm the time
quests.textToSpeak: I’m calling to confirm the time
options: /tuː/: a long full vowel, because the speaker is being polite
/tɒ/: a short stressed vowel
/tuː/ with a /w/ glide before “confirm”
/tə/: a weak vowel, linking “calling” to “confirm” smoothly
quests.correctAnswer: /tə/: a weak vowel, linking “calling” to “confirm” smoothly
quests.hint: Say the sentence as you would on a call, and listen to the vowel in the word between “calling” and “confirm”.
quests.explanation: Infinitive “to” is unstressed before a verb and is reduced to /tə/: “I’m calling tuh confirm the time”. The strong /tuː/ appears at the end of a clause or under stress. The weak form helps the speaker keep a steady rhythm.
quests.phoneticRule: Infinitive “to” takes the weak form /tə/ before a verb; it keeps /tuː/ only when it is stressed or final.
quests.spokenForm: I’m calling tuh confirm thuh time

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “for a” fits “Hold for a moment, please”?
options: “for-ay”: both words are strong, with a clear break between them and no linking
“fore-uh”: “for” is strong and “a” is weak
“fuh-ruh”: both words are weak, with a linking /r/ before the vowel
“fuh-a”: “for” is weak but “a” keeps the full vowel /eɪ/
quests.correctAnswer: “fuh-ruh”: both words are weak, with a linking /r/ before the vowel
quests.hint: Say the phrase as a receptionist would, quickly, and notice how many full vowels you really use.
quests.explanation: “For” and “a” are both unstressed, so each takes a weak form: /fər ə/. Before the vowel of “a”, the British model adds a linking /r/: “fuh-ruh”. The only strong word is “moment”. Phone phrases like this are everywhere, so recognising the shape helps you follow quickly.
quests.phoneticRule: Two adjacent function words are both reduced, and the preposition “for” takes the linking form /fər/ before a vowel.

quests.instruction: Predict how “it to the” is said in “Forward it to the team”.
options: “it”, “to” and “the” are weak, so it sounds like “forwar-dit tuh thuh team”
Each of the three words is stressed to show the order of the task clearly to the team
Only “to” is weak; “it” and “the” keep full vowels
“it” is stressed because it refers to a document
quests.correctAnswer: “it”, “to” and “the” are weak, so it sounds like “forwar-dit tuh thuh team”
quests.hint: Ask which words you would remove if you had to write the instruction as a three-word note.
quests.explanation: In an instruction, the verb and the noun carry the stress, and the little words between them are reduced: “Forward-dit tuh thuh TEAM”. The /d/ of “forward” also links onto “it”. Predicting the weak words in advance makes it easier to follow quick instructions at work.
quests.phoneticRule: Function words between a verb and its object are typically unstressed, and “it” links to the preceding consonant.

quests.instruction: Why is “are” reduced in “Reports are due by Friday”?
options: “Are” is an unstressed auxiliary between stressed words, so its vowel becomes /ə/
“Are” is replaced by the word “a” in fast speech, so no /r/ is heard
“Are” is dropped completely, because the sentence is in the present tense and the meaning is clear
“Are” is stressed, which makes its /r/ shorter and its vowel reduced
quests.correctAnswer: “Are” is an unstressed auxiliary between stressed words, so its vowel becomes /ə/
quests.hint: Find the stressed words on either side of “are”. What happens to a small word squeezed between them?
quests.explanation: “Reports” and “due” carry the meaning, so they are stressed, and “are” sits between them with no stress of its own. It reduces to /ə/: “Reports uh due”. In the British model no /r/ is pronounced before a consonant. If it were stressed, you would hear /ɑː/.
quests.phoneticRule: Auxiliary “are” reduces to /ə/ between stressed words; the full /ɑː/ appears only under stress or at the end of a clause.

quests.instruction: Which words are weak in “I’ll get back to you by Friday”?
quests.word: I’ll get back to you by Friday
quests.textToSpeak: I’ll get back to you by Friday
options: “get”, “back” and “Friday” are weak; “to”, “you” and “by” are strong
Only “to” and “by” are weak
Every word is strong, because business English avoids reductions
“to”, “you” and “by” are weak; “get”, “back” and “Friday” are strong
quests.correctAnswer: “to”, “you” and “by” are weak; “get”, “back” and “Friday” are strong
quests.hint: Mark the three words that carry the message, then see which of the others can be said quietly.
quests.explanation: The message is “get back… Friday”, so those words are stressed. The pronoun and prepositions around them are quiet: “I’ll get BACK tuh yuh buh FRIDAY”. Business English uses weak forms just as everyday English does; clarity comes from stress, not from full vowels everywhere.
quests.phoneticRule: Professional speech keeps the same weak forms as casual speech; clarity is created by stress on content words rather than by full forms.
quests.spokenForm: I’ll get back tuh yuh buh Friday

quests.instruction: At university you ask, “Where’s the exam?” Which spoken form of “the” fits?
options: /ðə/: the weak form that is used before consonants such as /b/ or /k/
/ðiː/: a stressed, long vowel to mark which exam the speaker means
/ði/: the form before a vowel, often with a /j/ glide: “thee-yexam”
/θiː/: with a voiceless first sound, as in “thin”
quests.correctAnswer: /ði/: the form before a vowel, often with a /j/ glide: “thee-yexam”
quests.hint: Check the first sound of “exam”, then recall the two forms of “the”.
quests.explanation: “Exam” begins with a vowel sound, so “the” is /ði/ and a light /j/ glide often links the two vowels: “Where’s thee-yexam”. Before a consonant it would be /ðə/. Hearing this tells you that the next word starts with a vowel, which is a useful clue in fast speech.
quests.phoneticRule: The form /ði/ before vowel-initial words signals that a vowel follows, and it is often linked by a /j/ glide.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form fits “Lectures start at nine or ten”?
quests.word: Lectures start at nine or ten
quests.textToSpeak: Lectures start at nine or ten
options: “at” is /æt/ and “or” is /ɔː/, both with full vowels
“at” is /ət/ and “or” is /ə/, so it sounds like “at nine uh ten”
“at” is /ət/ but “or” keeps /ɔː/ because it joins numbers
Both are dropped, so it sounds like “start nine ten”
quests.correctAnswer: “at” is /ət/ and “or” is /ə/, so it sounds like “at nine uh ten”
quests.hint: Say the sentence quickly and notice which two small words are almost swallowed.
quests.explanation: Both “at” and “or” are function words, so they reduce to /ət/ and /ə/. The numbers “nine” and “ten” carry the information and are stressed: “Lectures START uht NINE uh TEN”. Timetables are full of such patterns, so recognising the weak words helps you catch the times.
quests.phoneticRule: Prepositions and conjunctions between numbers or names are reduced; the numbers themselves carry the stress.
quests.spokenForm: Lectures start uht nine uh ten

quests.instruction: In “Were you at the lecture?”, which word carries the main stress in a neutral question?
options: “were”, because it starts the question
“you”, because it is the subject
“at”, because it shows the place
“lecture”
quests.correctAnswer: “lecture”
quests.hint: Ask which word carries the information the speaker is asking about.
quests.explanation: The question is about the lecture, so “lecture” carries the stress. “Were”, “you”, “at” and “the” are all weak: /wə/, /jə/, /ət/, /ðə/. Stress shows where the new information is, and the rest is reduced to a quiet background.
quests.phoneticRule: In neutral questions, stress falls on the content word that carries new information, and the surrounding function words are weak.

quests.instruction: At a shop you ask “How much is it for a pair?” Which statement fits the words “is it for a”?
quests.word: How much is it for a pair
quests.textToSpeak: How much is it for a pair
options: All four are reduced and run together as “iz-it fuh-ruh”
Only “is” and “it” are reduced; “for” and “a” stay strong
Only “for” and “a” are reduced; “is” and “it” stay strong
None: price questions are stressed word by word
quests.correctAnswer: All four are reduced and run together as “iz-it fuh-ruh”
quests.hint: Look for the stressed words (how much, pair) and treat the four words between them as background.
quests.explanation: In the question, “how much” and “pair” are stressed. The four small words between them are reduced to “iz-it fuh-ruh”, with a linking /r/ before the weak “a” in the British model. Shoppers who expect each word clearly can lose the question, so it helps to listen for the stressed words first.
quests.phoneticRule: A string of consecutive function words is typically reduced as a block, producing a rapid unstressed stretch between stressed words.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “of” fits “Got any of these in blue?”
quests.word: Got any of these in blue
quests.textToSpeak: Got any of these in blue
options: /ɒv/: a full vowel, because “of” follows “any”
/ɒf/: a full vowel with an /f/ at the end
/əv/ or /ə/: a weak vowel, so it sounds like “any-uv these”
/ʌv/: a stressed vowel like the one in “love”
quests.correctAnswer: /əv/ or /ə/: a weak vowel, so it sounds like “any-uv these”
quests.hint: Say “got any of these” quickly and listen to the vowel in the word that follows “any”.
quests.explanation: “Of” is an unstressed preposition, so it reduces to /əv/, and “any of” can sound like “any-uv”. The full vowel /ɒv/ is used only when “of” is stressed. Recognising weak “of” also helps you hear spoken English as a series of linked small words.
quests.phoneticRule: Weak “of” is /əv/ after quantifiers such as “any” and “some”, and the stressed vowel /ɒv/ is rare in connected speech.
quests.spokenForm: Got any uv these in blue

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “than” fits “Cheaper than the others”?
options: /ðæn/: a full vowel with strong stress, because it compares
/ðən/: a weak vowel, so it sounds like “cheaper thun”
/θæn/: a voiceless first sound
/dæn/: a /d/ instead of /ð/
quests.correctAnswer: /ðən/: a weak vowel, so it sounds like “cheaper thun”
quests.hint: Listen to how long the vowel in “than” lasts compared with the vowel in “cheap-”.
quests.explanation: “Than” is a function word and is normally unstressed: /ðən/. The comparison is carried by “cheaper” and “others”, which are stressed. The full /ðæn/ appears when “than” is stressed, for instance at the end of a clause. Also note that “the” becomes /ði/ before “others”.
quests.phoneticRule: “Than” is weak (/ðən/) in ordinary comparisons, with stress on the adjective and on the compared item.

quests.instruction: Which pair of words is reduced in the announcement “Trains to Leeds leave from platform four”?
quests.word: Trains to Leeds leave from platform four
quests.textToSpeak: Trains to Leeds leave from platform four
options: “Leeds” and “four”, which are the least important words
“leave” and “platform”, which are verbs
None of them, because station announcements are spoken slowly
“to” and “from”, which take weak forms /tə/ and /frəm/
quests.correctAnswer: “to” and “from”, which take weak forms /tə/ and /frəm/
quests.hint: Remove the words that give the place names and numbers, and see which small words are left.
quests.explanation: In announcements the stressed words are the destination, the verb, the place and the number: “TRAINS tuh LEEDS LEAVE frum PLATform FOUR”. The words “to” and “from” are prepositions and are reduced. Even slow announcements keep weak forms, so learning them helps you catch details.
quests.phoneticRule: Prepositions such as “to” and “from” keep weak forms in public announcements, whereas place names, numbers and verbs carry the stress.
quests.spokenForm: Trains tuh Leeds leave frum platform four

quests.instruction: How are “to” and “the” pronounced in “Which bus goes to the airport?”
quests.word: Which bus goes to the airport
quests.textToSpeak: Which bus goes to the airport
options: “to” is /tə/ and “the” is /ði/ before the vowel of “airport”
“to” is /tuː/ and “the” is /ðə/, as before a consonant
“to” is /tə/ and “the” is /ðə/, because “the” has only one weak form
Both are dropped, so it sounds like “goes airport”
quests.correctAnswer: “to” is /tə/ and “the” is /ði/ before the vowel of “airport”
quests.hint: Look at the first sound of “airport” and recall what it does to the word before it.
quests.explanation: “To” is unstressed before a noun phrase and reduces to /tə/. “The” changes to /ði/ because “airport” begins with a vowel, so the sentence is heard as “tuh thee-yairport”. Two earlier ideas, weak forms and the vowel form of “the”, appear together in an everyday travel question.
quests.phoneticRule: Weak “to” and vowel-form “the” can occur together: /tə ði/ before vowel-initial nouns.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form fits “How far is it to Leeds?”
quests.word: How far is it to Leeds
quests.textToSpeak: How far is it to Leeds
options: “how far is it too Leeds”: every word has a full vowel
“how far iz it to Leeds”: only “to” keeps its full vowel
“how far-riz it tuh Leeds”: a linking /r/, then weak “it” and “to”
“how fah is it tuh Leeds”: no /r/ is heard before “is”, and “is” stays strong
quests.correctAnswer: “how far-riz it tuh Leeds”: a linking /r/, then weak “it” and “to”
quests.hint: Check the end of “far” and decide whether a vowel comes next, then recall what the British model does in that case.
quests.explanation: “Far” ends in a spelled “r” and “is” begins with a vowel, so a linking /r/ appears: “far-riz”. “It” and “to” are function words and are weak. The stressed words are “far” and “Leeds”. So the sentence combines a linking /r/ with two weak forms.
quests.phoneticRule: Stage 2 linking and Stage 5 weak forms operate together: a linking /r/ attaches to the following weak word.

quests.instruction: In “Stand at the back”, what explains the /d/ joining “at” as “stan-dət”?
options: Only a weak form: “at” is reduced, so the /d/ moves onto it
Both: the /d/ links onto “at”, and “at” itself is reduced to /ət/
Only linking: “at” keeps its full vowel /æt/ and the /d/ moves
Neither: the words are separated by a short pause, so nothing changes
quests.correctAnswer: Both: the /d/ links onto “at”, and “at” itself is reduced to /ət/
quests.hint: Separate two questions: what happens to the /d/, and what happens to the vowel of “at”.
quests.explanation: The /d/ moves onto “at” because a vowel follows: that is linking. Separately, “at” is a function word with a weak vowel: that is a weak form. The two processes are independent but often occur together: “stan-dət”.
quests.phoneticRule: Linking changes which syllable a consonant belongs to, while weak forms change the quality of a vowel; both can apply to the same word.

quests.instruction: In “Shop for shoes”, “for” is reduced to /fə/. Is this linking or a weak form?
options: Linking: the /p/ of “shop” moves onto “for” and forms the first syllable of the next word
A weak form: only the vowel changes, since “shoes” begins with a consonant
Linking: the /r/ of “for” moves onto the start of the word “shoes”
Elision: the whole word “for” is omitted, so “shop shoes” is heard
quests.correctAnswer: A weak form: only the vowel changes, since “shoes” begins with a consonant
quests.hint: Check the sounds on both sides of “for”: is there a consonant followed by a vowel anywhere?
quests.explanation: “Shop” ends in /p/ and “for” begins with /f/, so there is no vowel to link to. After “for” comes “shoes”, which begins with a consonant, so no linking /r/ appears either. The only change is the reduced vowel, so this is a pure weak form.
quests.phoneticRule: A weak form without linking is identified when neither side of the function word offers a consonant-to-vowel boundary.

quests.instruction: Which description fits “Stop at a café”?
options: The /p/ links onto “at”, “at” is weak, and its /t/ links onto the weak “a”
“at” is strong, so no link is possible between “stop” and “at”
Only the weak forms occur; no consonant moves onto a following vowel
Only linking occurs; “at” and “a” keep their full vowels, as in careful speech and dictation
quests.correctAnswer: The /p/ links onto “at”, “at” is weak, and its /t/ links onto the weak “a”
quests.hint: Count the consonant + vowel boundaries, then check which of the small words are weak.
quests.explanation: The /p/ of “stop” meets the vowel of “at”, so it links. “At” and “a” are function words, so both are reduced, and the /t/ of “at” links onto the weak “a”: “sto-pə-tə café”. Both processes occur twice in one short phrase, which is why fast speech seems so smooth.
quests.phoneticRule: In sequences of weak function words, linking and vowel reduction apply together and create a chain of shifted consonants and reduced vowels.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “ask her” fits “Ask her to call back”?
options: “ask … her”: a clear /h/ after a pause
“ask-sher”: the /h/ becomes a “sh” sound
“ask-her”: the /h/ is dropped but a pause stays between the words
“as-kər”: the /h/ is dropped, and the /k/ links to the weak “her”
quests.correctAnswer: “as-kər”: the /h/ is dropped, and the /k/ links to the weak “her”
quests.hint: Say “ask her” as part of the sentence, and notice what the /k/ seems to start.
quests.explanation: In an unstressed pronoun after another word, the /h/ is often dropped: “as-ker”. The /k/ of “ask” then links onto the weak vowel. The same pattern appears in appointments and messages, where requests like this are common.
quests.phoneticRule: Unstressed “her” loses its /h/ after another word and is reduced to /ə/, so the preceding consonant links onto it.

quests.instruction: In “Dr Lee said he’d call”, what happens to the /h/ of “he’d”?
options: It is kept clearly, because “he’d” follows a short pause
It is replaced by a /j/ glide
It is often dropped, so “said he’d” sounds like “sed-eed”
It is moved onto the end of “said”
quests.correctAnswer: It is often dropped, so “said he’d” sounds like “sed-eed”
quests.hint: Think about whether “he’d” is stressed here, and what follows “said” in the sentence.
quests.explanation: “He’d” follows “said” and is unstressed, so its /h/ is often dropped: “sed-eed”. Appointment messages are full of such patterns, which is why they can sound cryptic to learners at first.
quests.phoneticRule: In reported speech, an unstressed subject pronoun after the verb of saying commonly loses its /h/.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “his” fits “Cancel his appointment, please”?
options: “can-səliz”: the /h/ is dropped, and the /l/ links onto “his”
“cancel his”: the /h/ is kept clearly
“cancel-chis”: the /h/ becomes a “ch” sound
“cancel-iss”: the /h/ is dropped and the /z/ becomes /s/
quests.correctAnswer: “can-səliz”: the /h/ is dropped, and the /l/ links onto “his”
quests.hint: Look at how “cancel” ends and what the weak “his” begins with once the /h/ is gone.
quests.explanation: After the /h/ is dropped, “his” begins with a vowel, so the /l/ of “cancel” attaches to it: “can-səliz”. The /z/ stays voiced. Clinic and office staff say this quickly, so recognising the pattern helps you understand changes to bookings.
quests.phoneticRule: The /h/ of unstressed “his” is often dropped, and the final consonant of the preceding word links to the resulting vowel-initial form.

quests.instruction: Which features are heard in “Tell them to wait”?
options: Elision of the /l/ and a strong “to”
Assimilation of the /l/ to /m/ before a strong “them” that keeps its /ð/
A weak “them” (/əm/) linked to “tell”, and a weak “to” (/tə/)
Only linking: every word keeps its full vowel
quests.correctAnswer: A weak “them” (/əm/) linked to “tell”, and a weak “to” (/tə/)
quests.hint: Listen to the small words and decide which ones are weak, and which consonant joins a weak word.
quests.explanation: “Them” is weak (/əm/) and begins with a vowel once the /ð/ is lost, so the /l/ of “tell” links to it: “te-ləm”. “To” is also weak: /tə/. So the phrase shows pronoun reduction, linking and a second weak form together.
quests.phoneticRule: Pronoun reduction and linking commonly co-occur: a weak pronoun with a lost initial consonant is a vowel-initial word that takes the previous consonant.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “email him” fits “Email him when it’s done”?
options: “email … him”: both words are strong, with a clear pause and a clear /h/ between them
“email-chim”: the /h/ becomes a “ch” sound
“emai-him”: the /l/ is dropped and the /h/ is kept
“emai-lim”: the /h/ is dropped and the /l/ links onto the weak “him”
quests.correctAnswer: “emai-lim”: the /h/ is dropped and the /l/ links onto the weak “him”
quests.hint: Say “email him” quickly and listen to what the last sound of “email” does.
quests.explanation: The /h/ of “him” is dropped, so “him” is /ɪm/, and the /l/ of “email” links onto it: “emai-lim”. The rest of the sentence continues normally. This is the same combined pattern you heard in “Tell them to wait”, now with a different pronoun.
quests.phoneticRule: The combination of /h/ dropping and linking is not specific to one pronoun: it applies to him, her, his and them alike.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form fits “Show us the way”?
options: “show-yus”: a /j/ glide links the two words
“show-wus”: a /w/ glide links “show” to the weak “us” (/əs/)
“show-rus”: a linking /r/ links the two words
“show us”: both words are strong, with a pause
quests.correctAnswer: “show-wus”: a /w/ glide links “show” to the weak “us” (/əs/)
quests.hint: Check the last sound of “show” and remember which glide follows a rounded vowel.
quests.explanation: “Show” ends in a rounded vowel, so a light /w/ bridges to the weak “us”: “show-wus”. That glide comes from the vowel-to-vowel linking you learned earlier, and the weak /əs/ comes from the weak-form rules. Both are at work in four short words.
quests.phoneticRule: Glide linking applies to weak vowel-initial pronouns, with the glide chosen by the ending of the preceding vowel.

quests.instruction: A friend says Anna hasn’t told Beth. You reply, “Anna HAS told her!” How is “has” pronounced?
options: As a strong /hæz/, with a clear /h/, because it carries contrastive stress
As a weak /əz/ or /z/, as in the neutral and unstressed sentence “Anna’s told her”
As /hɑːz/, with a long vowel and no stress at all
As /hæs/, with a voiceless final consonant and a clear /h/
quests.correctAnswer: As a strong /hæz/, with a clear /h/, because it carries contrastive stress
quests.hint: You are correcting a negative claim. Which word do you stress to do that?
quests.explanation: To contradict “hasn’t”, the speaker stresses the auxiliary, and a stressed auxiliary takes its strong form: /hæz/, with a clear /h/. In a neutral statement it would be reduced to /əz/. Listening for the strong form signals that the speaker is correcting or emphasising.
quests.phoneticRule: Contrastive stress restores the full vowel and the initial /h/ of auxiliaries such as “has”, which are otherwise weak.

quests.instruction: When is “can” likely to be pronounced /kæn/ in “Lee can swim”?
options: Whenever the sentence is a statement about what someone can do
When it is stressed, for example to contradict “Lee can’t swim”
Whenever the sentence is spoken slowly and clearly to a listener
When “can” follows a name at the start of a sentence
quests.correctAnswer: When it is stressed, for example to contradict “Lee can’t swim”
quests.hint: Think about why someone would put extra weight on a small word in the middle of a sentence.
quests.explanation: The strong form /kæn/ is a marker of emphasis. In a neutral “Lee can swim”, “can” is weak, /kən/. Speaking slowly makes weak forms longer but does not turn them into strong ones, and the position after a name has no effect. So the reason is contrast, not speed or position.
quests.phoneticRule: A strong form in the middle of a clause usually marks contrast or emphasis, not slow speech or grammatical position.

quests.instruction: Someone gives the gift to the wrong person: “Those are for HER, not him!” How is “her” pronounced?
quests.word: Those are for her, not him
quests.textToSpeak: Those are for her, not him
options: As a weak /ə/, with no /h/ and a very short vowel
As /hə/, with a clear /h/ but a weak vowel
As /hiː/, like the word “he”, said with extra emphasis on the vowel
As a strong /hɜː/, with a clear /h/ and a full vowel
quests.correctAnswer: As a strong /hɜː/, with a clear /h/ and a full vowel
quests.hint: The speaker is contrasting two people; decide which of the two pronouns gets the stress.
quests.explanation: In a contrast, the pronoun that identifies the right person takes the stress and its strong form: /hɜː/. The weak /ə/ would suggest that “her” is just background. Hearing the full form tells you which person the speaker means.
quests.phoneticRule: Pronouns in contrast take strong forms with a full vowel and a clear /h/, even though the weak forms are the default.
quests.spokenForm: Those uh fuh HER, not him

quests.instruction: At a restaurant you say, “Table for two, please.” Which spoken form fits “table for two”?
options: “table for two”, with every word at full strength
“table fuh too”: “for” is /fə/ and “two” is reduced as well
“table fuh two”: “for” is weak and “two” keeps its full stress
“table four two”: “for” is strong, like the number
quests.correctAnswer: “table fuh two”: “for” is weak and “two” keeps its full stress
quests.hint: Decide which of the three words carries the information, and which is only a joining word.
quests.explanation: “Table” and “two” are the information, so both are stressed. “For” is a preposition and is weak: /fə/. The word “two” cannot be reduced like “to” because it is a number and carries meaning. This tells you that weak forms depend on a word’s job, not its spelling.
quests.phoneticRule: Homophones can behave differently in stress: the prepositions “for” and “to” are weak, while the numbers “four” and “two” are content words and stay strong.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “Bring them to the office” fits fast speech?
options: “bring əm tuh thee-yoffice”: “them” and “to” are weak, and “the” is /ði/
“bring them too the office”: “them” and “to” are strong and “the” is /ðə/
“bring ’em tuh thuh office”: “the” is /ðə/ before a vowel
“bringem-to-the-office”: every word is dropped except “bring”
quests.correctAnswer: “bring əm tuh thee-yoffice”: “them” and “to” are weak, and “the” is /ði/
quests.hint: Check each small word in turn: them, to, the. Which form does each one take?
quests.explanation: “Them” and “to” are unstressed, so they reduce to /əm/ and /tə/, and “the” becomes /ði/ before the vowel of “office”. Only “bring” and “office” carry the stress. The sentence therefore combines three weak-form ideas from this stage.
quests.phoneticRule: A single sentence can combine pronoun reduction, weak “to”, and the vowel form of “the”; each is chosen by its own context.

quests.instruction: Which features are heard in “Remember to call him back”?
options: A strong “to”, a clear /h/ in “him” and a pause before it, with no linking at all
A weak “to” (/tə/), a dropped /h/ in “him”, and the /l/ linking onto it
Elision of the /l/ in “call” and a strong “him”
Only a weak “to”; “him” is unchanged
quests.correctAnswer: A weak “to” (/tə/), a dropped /h/ in “him”, and the /l/ linking onto it
quests.hint: List each small word and decide whether it is weak; then check what happens at the boundary between “call” and “him”.
quests.explanation: “To” is weak, “him” loses its /h/ and is /ɪm/, and the /l/ of “call” links onto it: “caw-lim”. The stressed words are “remember”, “call” and “back”. This stage-check sentence combines weak forms, /h/ dropping and linking, which is the real shape of fast English.
quests.phoneticRule: Realistic sentences combine weak forms, /h/ dropping and linking, so each boundary is analysed for all three.
